content.overview: Section 13 provides the procedural route for challenging an arbitrator after appointment, including written reasons, statutory timing and first-instance determination by the tribunal.
content.glance: Section 13 provides the procedural route for challenging an arbitrator after appointment, including written reasons, statutory timing and first-instance determination by the tribunal.
content.study:
Module 1: Written challenge
A party intending to challenge must send a written statement of reasons within the statutory period after becoming aware of the relevant circumstance.

Module 2: First-instance decision
Unless the challenged arbitrator withdraws or the other party agrees, the arbitral tribunal determines the challenge.

Module 3: Advocacy
A proper challenge identifies the statutory ground, establishes timeliness and distinguishes independence concerns from dissatisfaction with procedural rulings.

examples.title: Rule applies
examples.body: A party promptly discovers a relevant circumstance and serves a written challenge within the statutory period.

examples.title: Rule fails or changes
examples.body: A party complains about an adverse procedural order without establishing a statutory challenge ground.

hypotheticals.question: How does section 13 differ from section 12?
hypotheticals.analysis: Section 12 supplies the substantive disclosure/challenge framework; section 13 supplies the procedural route.

misconceptions.trap: Treating section 13 as an automatic substitute for the surrounding statutory framework.
misconceptions.correction: Apply section 13 with its express conditions and neighbouring provisions.
